name: Apphia (Philemon's wife?)
title: Fellow Christian and possible hostess in Colossae
summary: In the opening greeting of the letter to Philemon, Paul addresses three named individuals: Philemon, Apphia and Archippus, as well as the house church that gathers in their home. Apphia is referred to as 'our sister' – an expression that marks her as a recognized fellow believer. The traditional interpretation, which can be traced back to the early church, identifies her as Philemon's wife. This understanding is supported by the context of the letter: it concerns the fate of the runaway slave Onesimus, a matter that affected the entire household. That Paul chooses to include Apphia as a recipient in an otherwise very personal letter suggests that her voice and consent were significant. As a possible hostess for the house church in Colossae, she represents the many women in the early church who opened their homes for Christian gatherings and thus contributed substantially to the life and spread of the congregation.
roles: possible co-leader of the house church

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as a recipient in the Letter to Philemon
keyEvents.description: Paul addresses his letter to Philemon, Apphia ('our sister'), and Archippus, as well as the house church that meets with them. The fact that Apphia is named as a recipient in a personal letter concerning the runaway slave Onesimus indicates that she held a central position in both the household and the congregation, and that her consent to the matter was important to Paul.

versions.summary: Apphia is mentioned in Paul's Letter to Philemon as one of the recipients along with Philemon and Archippus. She is referred to as 'our sister' and is traditionally believed to have been Philemon's wife. She was part of the house church in Colossae.
versions.title: Sister in the faith
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Sister in Faith' is fine, but could have been more descriptive. Paul calls her 'our sister' (Greek: adelphē), and she was likely part of the leadership in the house church. A title such as 'Sister in Faith Mentioned in Philemon' or 'Fellow Believer in the Colossian House Church' would provide more context.; [major] The role 'servant' is not directly attested in the text. The Bible calls her 'our sister' (adelphē), which is a term for a fellow believer. There is no biblical evidence that she was a 'servant' in any formal sense. More appropriate roles would be 'fellow believer', 'house church member', or possibly 'hostess'.; [minor] The connection to Philemon as her spouse is traditional but not explicitly confirmed in the biblical text. It is a reasonable assumption, but should be reflected as uncertain. The profile already has a question mark in the name field, which is good.; [minor] Traditionally, many scholars have assumed that Archippus may have been the son of Philemon and Apphia, based on the order in the greeting (Philemon, Apphia, Archippus). Although this is uncertain, it could have been mentioned as a possibility, for example with Archippus in the children array.; [minor] The two key events are very similar and overlap significantly – both concern Apphia being mentioned in Philemon verses 1–2. They could usefully be merged into one more detailed event, or the second could focus on another dimension.; [minor] The summary is good, but could be expanded somewhat with information that her inclusion in the letter's addressee list may indicate a leadership role in the house church, and that her mention in connection with the Onesimus case may suggest that as the mistress of the house she had an interest in the outcome.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For such a little-mentioned person, it is important to have linguistic, historical, and theological context notes – for example about the Greek name Apphia, the tradition regarding her relationship with Philemon, and the house church structure in the early church.

footnotes.text: The name Apphia (Greek: Ἀπφία) is a Phrygian name that was widespread in Asia Minor, especially in the region of Phrygia where Colossae was located. The name is attested in numerous ancient inscriptions from the area, which confirms its local roots and makes it likely that Apphia was from this region.

When Paul calls Apphia 'our sister' (Greek: tēn adelphēn), this is the usual term for a female fellow believer in Pauline usage. The use of the definite article may indicate that she was a known and respected person in the church.

The tradition that Apphia was Philemon's wife goes back to the Church Father John Chrysostom (c. 349–407) and is the dominant interpretation among commentators. The context – that she is mentioned between Philemon and Archippus in a letter about a household matter – supports this view, but it remains an assumption.

House churches (Greek: kat' oikon ekklēsia) were the primary form of Christian gathering in the first century. Women as mistresses of the house often played a significant role in these congregations, as we also see with Lydia (Acts 16:40) and Nympha (Col 4:15).

According to a later church tradition, Apphia, Philemon, and Archippus all suffered martyrdom in Colossae during persecutions, possibly under Emperor Nero. This tradition is not historically verifiable, but Apphia is remembered as a saint in the Orthodox Church on November 22.

The fact that Apphia is specifically named as a recipient in a letter concerning the runaway slave Onesimus suggests she had a direct interest in the matter. In the Roman household system, the mistress (domina) had daily oversight of the slaves and servants, which further supports the interpretation that she was the mother of the household.

Some scholars have suggested that Archippus, who is mentioned together with Philemon and Apphia, may have been their son. This interpretation is supported by the order in the greeting – father, mother, son – but remains speculative since Paul does not explicitly state any family relationship between the three.

Colossae was a city in the Lycus Valley in western Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), along with the neighboring cities of Laodicea and Hierapolis. In Paul's time, the city had lost much of its former significance but remained a center for a mixed population of Phrygians, Greeks, and Jews. Archaeological excavations in the area have uncovered inscriptions bearing the name Apphia, confirming that the name was common in the region.
